text: Lesson 19 gave you the policy — the why. This lesson gives you its necessary partner, the piece that makes a policy actually checkable: the data standard.

A standard offers the technical detail for executing a policy effectively. Where the policy states what's required and why, the standard defines the exact, concrete rule — formats, structures, terminologies, thresholds — that makes the requirement consistently achievable.

Following straight from last lesson's confidentiality policy, a companion standard might read: all customer account numbers must be 10 digits, starting with two letters identifying the region. Notice it doesn't restate why that matters — the policy already covered that. It just makes the rule checkable.

Standards typically fall into four categories. Format standards — exact structure for a field. Terminology standards — the one approved term for a concept, which the next lesson covers in full. Quality standards — a specific measurable threshold. And security standards — the exact control that satisfies a policy's security requirement.

Policy without a standard is too vague to apply consistently; a standard without a policy has no stated reason to exist. Next lesson goes deep on the terminology category — definitions and naming standards. See you there.
